The Conservatory has a relatively short life cycle of 25 to 30 years, requiring multiple
rebuilds since it was first constructed in 1931.
Today's building replicates that 1930s structure, which served as an entrance into a greenhouse
complex that was decommissioned and demolished in the 1980s.
Since then, the Conservatory has transitioned into an ornamental structure, primarily for
public enjoyment.
It has not served as an educational or research structure for the university in the past 15
years.
Today, the same structure issues that have consistently plagued the building have effectively
forced its closure for public safety.
We've commissioned multiple independent structural engineering teams to complete their own assessments
of the building.
These reports have come back unanimous.
A full rebuild of the structure is required to make it safe and fit for public use.
Its three main elements, wood, steel and glass, are all showing signs of needing extensive
replacement or enhancement.
Because the conservatory operates with a high humidity interior, the wood is subject to
constant rot and decay.
In fact, it's estimated that 10% or less of the wood is original due to its previous rebuilds
and limited life cycles.
Steel framework must be significantly reinforced to bring the building up to code and ensure
it can withstand winter weather conditions.
Our structural engineers have recommended adding three times more steel than currently
exists, which could impact the overall look and feel of the building.
Finally, all the glass will need to be upgraded and changed, which would remove any original
panes that may still remain.
